note: Extracted 13 September 2026 from a PubMed census of 72 records (selank-pubmed-2026-09), 32 of them in Russian; eleven journal abstracts (SRC-104, SRC-105, SRC-110 to SRC-118) and all five practitioner sources. TRANSLATION: every Russian-language source was read only through the English abstract PubMed indexes. No translation was performed, nothing is quoted from Russian text, and design details absent from an English abstract are recorded as not stated (owner decision D-07). Seeds, the Peptide Handbook, the cheat sheet and Hack Smith are cited by file page; Campbell by the book's page numbers. Molecular weight was checked by summing average residue masses for the printed sequence. Amounts appear only in protocol fields.

compound.shortDescription: A seven-amino-acid peptide built from the immune peptide tuftsin, developed in Moscow as an anti-anxiety drug. Russian trials compared it with benzodiazepines; no placebo-controlled trial in patients was found.
compound.simpleSummary:
Selank is a small lab-made peptide based on tuftsin, a natural fragment of an antibody involved in immune signalling, with three amino acids added for stability. It was developed at a Russian Academy of Sciences institute as a treatment for anxiety.

**It has been tested in Russian patients with anxiety.** In one randomised study, Selank relieved anxiety about as well as a benzodiazepine tranquilliser, and had some energising effects. In another, adding Selank to a benzodiazepine seemed to reduce that drug's side effects. This index could read these studies only through short English summaries, and none compared Selank with a placebo in patients.

**Several practitioner claims go further than the studies.** One book says Selank performs far better than benzodiazepines; the trial found them similar. Claims that it improves learning and memory in people rest, as one of those books itself admits, on rat studies and personal accounts. How much of a nasal dose reaches the body in people has not been measured in any study found.
compound.practitionerSummary: Selank (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro; earlier TP-7) is a heptapeptide analogue of tuftsin (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg) extended with Pro-Gly-Pro. It inhibits enkephalin-degrading enzymes of human plasma and serum in vitro at micromolar concentrations, and patients with generalised anxiety disorder showed shortened enkephalin half-life. In rats it changed expression of 45 of 84 neurotransmission genes in frontal cortex within 1 hour, correlating with GABA's effects, while in IMR-32 cells it had no direct effect on GABAergic gene mRNA but modified GABA's. Tritium-labelled Selank is degraded in plasma to TKPRP, TKP, RP and GP. Human studies (Russian-language, English abstracts): a randomised comparison with medazepam in 62 patients with GAD or neurasthenia (similar anxiolytic effect, additional antiasthenic and psychostimulant effects, enkephalin half-life changes); a comparison with phenazepam in 60 patients (anxiolytic effect persisting a week after the last dose); a randomised add-on to phenazepam in 70 patients (earlier response and fewer phenazepam adverse effects); serum Th1/Th2 cytokine changes after 14 days; and resting-state connectivity changes in healthy volunteers. No placebo-controlled patient trial, human pharmacokinetic study, dependence study or cognitive-outcome trial was identified. Seized preparations in Belgium contained Selank.
compound.unknownsSummary: Not established: efficacy against placebo in any anxiety disorder; replication outside Russia; human pharmacokinetics, including the nasal bioavailability figure a practitioner book attributes to the developers; absence of dependence or withdrawal, which is asserted but not studied in the records found; any cognitive benefit in people; the doses used in the clinical studies, which the English abstracts do not state; and anything about N-acetyl Selank amidate.

aliases.note: NOT this molecule: a modified form sold as a nootropic. No study of it was identified.

claims.claimText: Selank (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro) dose-dependently inhibits enzymatic hydrolysis of enkephalin in human plasma and serum in vitro, more potently than bacitracin and puromycin, and patients with generalised anxiety disorder, but not panic disorder or agoraphobia, showed shortened enkephalin half-life and reduced total enkephalinase activity.
claims.plainLanguageText: In the laboratory, Selank slows the breakdown of the body's own calming peptides in human blood. People with generalised anxiety had faster breakdown of those peptides.
claims.interpretationNotes: Proposed as the mechanism of its anxiolytic effect by the authors. A tube of plasma is not a person, and the patient measurement did not involve Selank.
claims.uncertaintyText: In vitro inhibition; association in patients; causal link not shown.

evidence.interpretation: Enkephalinase inhibition by Selank and enkephalin half-life in anxiety disorders.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: Sequence stated; serum enkephalinase inhibition alongside Semax.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: In a randomised comparison in 62 patients with generalised anxiety disorder or neurasthenia, Selank (30 patients) and medazepam (32 patients) had similar anxiolytic effects on Hamilton, Zung and CGI scales, and Selank also showed antiasthenic and psychostimulant effects, with enkephalin half-life rising during Selank treatment.
claims.plainLanguageText: In a Russian trial, Selank reduced anxiety about as much as a benzodiazepine tranquilliser.
claims.interpretationNotes: The strongest human evidence: randomised, active comparator, no placebo. Similar effect to a benzodiazepine is not the same as better.
claims.uncertaintyText: Blinding not stated in the English abstract; small; no placebo arm.

evidence.interpretation: Anxiolytic outcomes versus medazepam and enkephalin measures.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: In 60 patients with phobic-anxiety and somatoform disorders, Selank showed a pronounced anxiolytic effect lasting a week after the last dose, compared with phenazepam; in a randomised study of 70 patients, adding Selank to phenazepam produced an earlier response and fewer phenazepam adverse effects, including during withdrawal.
claims.plainLanguageText: Two more Russian studies found Selank helped anxiety, and that adding it to a benzodiazepine reduced that drug's side effects.
claims.interpretationNotes: Same clinical field; the add-on finding bears on practitioner claims of no dependence only indirectly, since it measured phenazepam's effects, not Selank's.
claims.uncertaintyText: Allocation stated only for the second study; blinding not stated; no placebo arm.

evidence.interpretation: Anxiolytic effect and tolerability compared with phenazepam.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: Phenazepam alone versus phenazepam with Selank: response timing and adverse effects.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: Selank suppressed IL-6 gene expression in peripheral blood cells of patients with depression in vitro but not in healthy controls, and serum Th1/Th2 cytokine balance changed in patients with generalised anxiety disorder or neurasthenia after 14 days of Selank.
claims.plainLanguageText: Selank changed some immune signalling markers in patients' blood.
claims.interpretationNotes: Supports practitioner immune claims at the level of biomarkers only.
claims.uncertaintyText: Small; clinical relevance of the cytokine changes not shown.

evidence.interpretation: Serum cytokines after 14 days of treatment and cell-culture IL-6 findings.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: In rats, Selank changed the expression of 45 of 84 neurotransmission genes in frontal cortex within 1 hour, in a pattern correlated with GABA's effects; in IMR-32 neuroblastoma cells it had no direct effect on GABAergic gene mRNA but largely suppressed the changes GABA produced.
claims.plainLanguageText: In rats and cells, Selank appears to interact with the brain's main calming signalling system, GABA, rather than acting on it directly.
claims.interpretationNotes: Consistent with the authors' hypothesis of allosteric GABA modulation; not a demonstration of receptor binding.
claims.uncertaintyText: Gene expression in rat tissue and a cell line.

evidence.interpretation: Frontal cortex gene expression after Selank or GABA.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: No direct GABAergic mRNA change; modification of GABA's effect.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: Tritium-labelled Selank is degraded in blood plasma to the pentapeptide TKPRP, the tripeptide TKP and the dipeptides RP and GP, and its brain pharmacokinetics were studied after intranasal administration in vivo.
claims.plainLanguageText: Selank is broken down quickly into smaller pieces in blood.
claims.interpretationNotes: The only pharmacokinetic work identified; the species for the in vivo part is not stated in the English abstract.

evidence.interpretation: Degradation products in plasma and intranasal brain pharmacokinetics by tritium labelling.

claims.claimText: In 52 healthy participants, Selank and Semax each produced changes in resting-state functional connectivity between the right amygdala and right temporal cortex compared with placebo.
claims.plainLanguageText: Brain scans in healthy volunteers showed changes in how an anxiety-related brain region connects with others after Selank.
claims.interpretationNotes: An imaging signal in healthy people, not an anxiety or cognitive outcome.

evidence.interpretation: Functional connectivity after Selank, Semax or placebo.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.plainLanguageText: Seized products contained Selank, and it is sold online.
claims.interpretationNotes: Product identity in two seized samples.

disagreements.topic: Whether Selank is better than benzodiazepines.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: One practitioner book says Selank performs far better than benzodiazepines. The randomised trial found its anti-anxiety effect similar to one.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The trial reported similar anxiolytic effects with additional antiasthenic effects; a later study reported fewer benzodiazepine side effects when Selank was added. Neither shows superiority on anxiety.
disagreements.resolutionBasis: The randomised comparison with medazepam (SRC-110) reports similar anxiolytic effects. The handbook's 'far better' is not supported by the held trial abstracts; the Peptide Handbook's 'comparable' matches them.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: None further for what the trials say; superiority would need a trial designed to show it.

positions.positionText: Numerous human trials show it performs far better than benzodiazepines.
Clinical studies report anxiolytic effects comparable to benzodiazepines.
The anxiolytic effects of Selank and medazepam were similar.

disagreements.topic: Whether Selank improves learning and memory in people.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: One guide describes Selank as improving focus and learning for professionals. Another practitioner book says those effects have only been confirmed in rats and anecdotes.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The more cautious practitioner source matches the census: no human cognitive-outcome study was identified.

positions.positionText: Improves focus, mental clarity and learning ability.
Learning and memory effects confirmed only by rat studies and anonymous testimonials.

disagreements.topic: How much intranasal Selank reaches the body.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: A practitioner book gives a precise nasal absorption figure and says the drug reaches the brain within minutes, attributing this to the developers. This index could not find the study.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The developers published a tritium-labelled pharmacokinetic method with intranasal brain data; its English abstract gives no bioavailability figure and does not name the species.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: The primary pharmacokinetic study, or a human study.

positions.positionText: High intranasal bioavailability and detection in plasma and brain within minutes, attributed to the developer institute.
Brain pharmacokinetics after intranasal administration were studied; plasma degradation products identified; no bioavailability figure in the abstract.

disagreements.topic: Whether N-acetyl Selank amidate is the same as Selank.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: A cheat sheet lists 'Selank or NA Selank Amidate' as interchangeable. They are different molecules, and the studies used plain Selank.
disagreements.explanationNotes: End-group modification creates a different molecule; a vendor quoted in a practitioner book prefers it without citing evidence.
disagreements.resolutionBasis: Primary sources describe Selank as Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro (SRC-118, SRC-105); N-acetyl Selank amidate carries additional end groups; no study of the modified form was identified.

positions.positionText: Selank or NA Selank Amidate, one schedule for both.

disagreements.topic: Whether Selank has been through clinical trials.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: Russian doctors have published controlled studies of Selank. A European drug-testing laboratory says, as far as it knows, it has not completed any clinical trials.
disagreements.explanationNotes: As for Semax: small Russian-language studies exist; whether they count as the laboratory meant is not established.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: A search of Russian trial registries and regulatory dossiers.

positions.positionText: Reports a randomised comparison with medazepam.
To the authors' knowledge, Selank and Semax have not completed any clinical trials.

replication.finding: Selank has an anxiolytic effect in anxiety disorders.
replication.models: Adults with generalised anxiety disorder, neurasthenia, phobic-anxiety and somatoform disorders.
replication.basis: Three Moscow studies from 2008 to 2015. Lead authors differ between the 2008 and later studies, but institutional independence from the developer is not established from the abstracts, so the same-group state is recorded.
replication.limitations: No placebo arm; English abstracts only.

replication.finding: Selank inhibits enkephalin-degrading enzymes of human blood.
replication.models: Human plasma and serum in vitro.
replication.basis: Two 2001 reports from the same Moscow research centre.

replication.finding: Clinical effects of Selank outside Russia.
replication.basis: No human study outside Russia was identified.
